title: Given an array of positive integers, determine whether it can be split into two subsets with equal sums.
shortTitle: Partition Equal Subset Sum — subset-sum DP

s1_definition.profdef: Reduces to subset-sum: the array can be split equally if and only if the total is even and some subset sums to total/2. Use a boolean dp[s] meaning "sum s is reachable," initialize dp[0]=true, and for each number sweep s DOWNWARD updating dp[s] |= dp[s−num]. Time O(n · target), space O(target).
s1_definition.analogy: An auditor at National Bank of India wants to divide a set of transaction amounts into two piles of exactly equal total. If the grand total is odd this is impossible. Otherwise she checks whether some combination reaches half the total, because that half automatically leaves the other half behind.
s1_definition.oneliner: Total even and a subset hits total/2; boolean dp swept downward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reduces to subset-sum: the array can be split equally if and only if the total is even and some subset sums to total/2. Use a boolean dp[s] meaning "sum s is reachable," initialize dp[0]=true, and for each number sweep s DOWNWARD updating dp[s] |= dp[s−num]. Time O(n · target), space O(target).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An auditor at National Bank of India wants to divide a set of transaction amounts into two piles of exactly equal total. If the grand total is odd this is impossible. Otherwise she checks whether some combination reaches half the total, because that half automatically leaves the other half behind.

**One line to remember:** Total even and a subset hits total/2; boolean dp swept downward.

sections.s2_technical:
First compute the total. If it is odd, return false immediately because two equal integer piles are impossible. Otherwise set target to total/2 and create a boolean dp of size target+1 with dp[0]=true, since a sum of zero is always reachable by taking nothing.

For each number, sweep s from target down to the number and set dp[s] to dp[s] OR dp[s−num]. For example: `for (int s = target; s >= num; s--) dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - num];`. The downward sweep is the same 0/1 trick as knapsack, ensuring each number is used at most once. The answer is dp[target].

The time is O(n · target) and space is O(target). A senior nuance is that this is exactly the 0/1 knapsack feasibility variant with weights equal to values, and if an actual partition is needed you backtrack through a two-dimensional table or keep parent flags.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an auditor must split a batch of settlement amounts into two equal halves for a two-way reconciliation. This is exactly how Partition Equal Subset Sum works.

Problem 2 — If the batch total is odd, no equal split exists, and otherwise only reaching exactly half matters. This is exactly why the problem reduces to a subset-sum feasibility check at half the total.

The mini-project builds a `ReconciliationSplitter`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input amounts are one, five, eleven, five.

Step 1: The total is twenty-two, which is even, so the target half is eleven.

Step 2: dp of zero is true and all other sums start false.

Step 3: Processing one makes sum one reachable; processing five makes sums five and six reachable.

Step 4: Processing eleven makes sum eleven directly reachable, so dp of eleven becomes true.

Step 5: The answer is true because eleven equals half the total, and the second example has odd-or-unreachable half so it returns false.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Partition Equal Subset Sum reduces cleanly to a subset-sum feasibility problem. The array can be split into two equal halves if and only if the total is even and some subset sums to exactly half the total, because that subset automatically leaves the other half behind. So I first check parity: if the total is odd I return false immediately.

For the feasibility test I use a boolean dynamic programming array where dp of s means the sum s is reachable. I initialize dp of zero to true because taking nothing reaches zero, and for each number I sweep the sums from the target down to the number, setting dp of s to itself or dp of s minus the number. The downward sweep is the same zero-one trick as the knapsack, so each number is used at most once, and the answer is dp of the target.

In my project at National Bank of India, an auditor needed to split a batch of settlement amounts into two equal halves for a two-way reconciliation. I recognized this as the zero-one knapsack feasibility variant where the weight equals the value, reduced it to reaching half the total, and solved it with a one-dimensional boolean table.
